title: A family of behaviours, pinned by a measurement
intro: An equation of change describes what is possible. One condition says what happened.

steps.title: Read it before solving it
steps.body:
**Order** is the highest derivative present and tells you how many arbitrary constants the general solution carries — and therefore how many conditions you need. **Degree** is the power of that highest derivative, but only when the equation is **polynomial in its derivatives**.

`y′ + cos(y′) = 0` has order 1 and **no degree at all**. The derivative is trapped inside a transcendental function, so the concept does not apply. 'Undefined' is the correct answer; a classifier that returns a number there is lying rather than failing.

points.label: Order
points.note: Highest derivative. Counts the arbitrary constants, hence how many measurements pin the solution down.

points.label: Degree
points.note: Power of that highest derivative — meaningful only if the equation is polynomial in its derivatives.

points.label: Undefined
points.note: y′ + cos(y′) = 0. Not zero, not one. The honest answer is that degree does not apply here.

steps.title: General, then particular
steps.body:
A second-order equation's general solution carries two arbitrary constants: a whole family of behaviours obeying the same physics. Supply `y(0) = 2` and `y′(0) = 4` and the family collapses to one curve, `y = 2e^(2x)`.

The reading is the same everywhere. The general solution is the family of conic **orbits**; the boundary conditions are *this* vehicle's position and velocity. The equation is the RLC **ring-down** shape; the conditions are the state at the instant the switch flipped.

steps.title: Verify by substituting, not by looking
steps.body:
Put the candidate back into the equation and simplify. The residual must be **exactly zero**.

A plausible wrong answer announces itself under this test — substituting sin(2x) into one of these leaves a residual of `-8·sin(2x)`, which is neither zero nor subtle. Checking a solution is mechanical and takes less time than second-guessing it.

steps.title: The two first-order moves
steps.body:
**Separable** — get it to `f(y) dy = g(x) dx` and integrate both sides. `dy/dx = -2xy` separates to `dy/y = -2x dx`, giving the Gaussian family `y = C·e^(-x²)`, with y(0) = 10 pinning C = 10.

**Homogeneous** — when every term shares the same total degree, the substitution `y = vx` *forces* separability. `dy/dx = (x + y)/x` collapses to `x·dv/dx = 1`, giving `y = x·ln|x| + Cx`.

Then the boundary condition makes it physical: RC discharge `V = 5e^(-1000t)` has τ = 1 ms, with the voltage at t = τ down to exactly `V₀/e ≈ 37%`. Barometric decay `P = 101.3·e^(-h/8.5)` kPa gives about **27.8 kPa** at 11 km — roughly a quarter of sea level.

recap: Order counts the constants you must supply; degree only exists when the equation is polynomial in its derivatives. The general solution is a family, and a measurement selects the member. Separable and homogeneous are the two first-order moves, and substitution is how you check you got it right.
